prize_parts.citation: For the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its development to the 10^-18 level, opening precision tests of gravity and many-body physics with atomic clocks

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. Having read the whole exchange, I find that the case rests on three things that no one has disputed. First, the idea is specific and has a named originator: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift while keeping thousands of atoms, which a trapped-atom clock cannot do without it. Second, the experimental claim is verified by direct comparison between independent laboratories at about 1e-18, not by one group's say-so. Third, the clock is no longer only a better ruler. Redshift tests across millimetres, bounds on the constancy of constants, and the many-body spin physics in the lattice are results about nature, and I want the citation to say so. This is the clue from nature that I keep asking for. The attribution is two names with an unusually clear division: Katori for the scheme and its first realisation, Ye for taking it to the highest precision and into many-body regimes. I did not move to B027 because six colleagues did; I moved because, on credit and on how settled the claim is, it holds up when I test it against the others.
statement.case_against: The overlap with 2005 and 2012 is the real objection and I will not wave it away. Hall and Hansch gave us the comb, and Wineland gave us control of single ions and the ion clock. Ye's early career sits next to the first and the lattice clock is an application of both in the eyes of a sceptical reader. My answer is that magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms is a distinct mechanism that neither prize covers, which is why the citation must name it and must name what the precision has shown, so that it cannot be read as a third metrology prize. A second objection is that the fundamental discoveries so far are tighter bounds and not a surprise, and the redefinition of the second has not happened. I do not think the committee should wait for the redefinition. That would reward an administrative decision, while the physics was settled by the comparisons. Finally, Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates are outside the credit. I regard that as a boundary of a two-person prize, and an ordinary one, but I admit that Ye's role is development rather than invention and the citation should say invention and development.

responses.point: Lindroth asked, in answer to my overlap argument, for a precise citation so the prize is not read as another general metrology prize, and she and Olsson both said that Ye's claim is a development case and Katori's the original invention.
responses.response: I accept both points and have changed the wording accordingly. The citation now names the magic-wavelength lattice clock and its development to 1e-18, and then the two things the precision has shown, tests of gravity and many-body clock physics. That is an honest statement of the roles: Katori is the inventor of the scheme, and Ye's decisive step was development, from the strontium clock at 1e-18 to the spin-exchange and many-body physics. I do not think that makes Ye a second-best-experiment laureate, because a lattice clock that works at that level is what turns the idea into a discovery that others could reproduce. As for Takamoto, Ludlow and Lemonde, I regard them as footnotes in the sense that the 2005 demonstration of the clock transition and the later JILA comparisons are part of what a two-name prize always leaves out, but I do not claim the footnote is small.

responses.point: Eriksson holds B057 first and says he would move the clock to the top rather than force an unsettled B057 if the committee finds the Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang question unresolved, and he argues that the 2016 prize concerns model systems while B057 concerns real band insulators.
responses.response: I take that answer seriously, and it is the best defence of B057 I have heard, since the distinction between topological phases in models and Z2 band topology in real materials is real. But my own test is the credit, and here it does not pass for me. The HgTe prediction that Molenkamp measured came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Zhang is dead, and no three-name configuration can include them together with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, nor the three-dimensional work of Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan. You said the citation could be framed around the Z2 concept and the observation, but then it would leave out the step that connected the two. I would respond differently if the committee were persuaded that the sequence of 2005, 2006 and 2007 can be told as one discovery with three clean names. I am not, and I think you are close to my view when you say you would move the clock up. I keep B057 as an alternative.

responses.point: Kroll argues that a clean credit is partly a consequence of a small number of people on a technique, that the clock is a tool rather than a change in what matter can be, and that the committee could wait without harming it. He also said the clock sits squarely in physics and is verified by direct comparison between independent clocks.
responses.response: I agree that a tidy attribution is not an argument for scientific importance, and I would not choose a prize for being tidy. But I disagree that this is only a tool. A tool that has already been used to see gravitational redshift over a millimetre, which is the equivalence principle at work in a laboratory sample, and to put limits on drifting constants, is producing results about nature. On waiting a cycle, I am less relaxed than you. The prize is not harmed by waiting, but nothing in the evidence changes by waiting either; the comparisons at 1e-18 already exist, and the redefinition of the second concerns the metrology community's decision. I would not tie the prize to it. You and I agree that the wording must carry the physics, and I would ask you to look at the new citation with that in mind.

responses.point: Pearce said that IceCube (B041) is the candidate he would pair with the clock if the committee wants two parts, that my reading of B041 is that it opened a window but the credited pair reflects leadership of a large project, and the chair asked whether B041 should remain a serious alternative.
responses.response: That is a fair account of my own hesitation. I still think B041 is the discovery that tells us most about the universe, and the 2013 evidence was a real step, but I will not argue for a two-part prize that adds Karle and Halzen to Katori and Ye. That would make four names, which exceeds the limit, and I think the committee would then have to drop one of the clock pair to fit, which weakens a clean credit in order to add a contested one. For one part, I also share your concern that source identification with TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 is still young and that the credit for a collaboration of hundreds is difficult. I keep it as an alternative, not as a second part, and would revisit it in a later year when the source picture has settled. I would be glad if you or Lindroth would say if you think that waiting is the wrong judgement.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B057 after moving from B008, argues that the 2016 overlap and the credit are the real weaknesses, and says B027 has the best attribution and timing on the list but should not be chosen merely for that reason.
responses.response: I think we agree about the weakness of B057 and differ in how much it matters. You describe it as a problem with the choice of names and not with the discovery, which is correct, but for the committee the names are the decision, since the statutes allow three at most and we must be able to defend each one. I also take your point about not letting a clean credit decide. What I would say for B027 is that the physics argument and the credit argument point the same way: a new mechanism, a new precision regime, and tests of gravity that follow from it. If B057 supporters can show that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp can be defended as the originators of the effect without a footnote on Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, I would move it to the top alternative, but I would need the committee, not my own memory of condensed-matter history, to establish that.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept the lattice clock as a distinct invention from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is the point on which my confidence is lowest; the citation wording is my only defence.

Whether Ye's role should be called invention or development, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are a footnote or a real attribution problem; I am not a specialist in atomic clocks and am relying on Lindroth and Kroll.
Whether the redefinition of the second should matter to timing; I think it should not, but others see it as supporting or deferring the case.
My condensed-matter judgement on B057 attribution is limited, and the committee may resolve it differently from me.
Whether IceCube (B041) is better left for later or should be acted on sooner.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited person or the shortlisted entries. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my co-author Thomas Van Riet work in string theory and cosmology, which is not related to the optical lattice clock or its credited names, Katori and Ye. I have no affiliation with JILA, RIKEN or Tokyo. I note again that Peter Zoller appears in B060 and B006, neither of which is in my configuration. Unchanged since round 1.
